A data point for the `GEOMETRY_REGEX` item, and two details that make it more than a quote class.

We consume a published format-version 3 catalog whose geometry fields carry the unquoted CRS, because that is what the engine writing them emits. PyIceberg 0.12.0 rejects the schema document:

```python
from pyiceberg.schema import Schema

Schema.model_validate_json(
    '{"type":"struct","schema-id":0,"fields":'
    '[{"id":1,"name":"geometry","required":false,"type":"geometry(EPSG:25830)"}]}'
```

@Fokko I looked into these two failures. pyparsing 3.3.3 replaced `infix_notation` with a new iterative implementation, and when an operand fails to parse it drops that error and raises a new one at the start of the operand. So it's not only the test wording: on 3.3.3 a bad row filter like `foo = ` used to report `Expected ... (at char 6)` and now reports a grammar dump at char 0. Upstream has a related open regression (pyparsing/pyparsing#672); a 3.3.4 was mentioned but hasn't been released.

Two options that work on both 3.3.2 and 3.3.3:

1. Write the NOT/AND/OR precedence explicitly with a `Forward` instead of `infix_notation` (~10 lines). The existing tests pass unchanged on both versions, and on 10k random filters it gave the same results and error positions as the current grammar. Trade-off: it doesn't get 3.3.3's support for very deeply nested parentheses.
2. Keep `infix_notation`, name the predicate so the 3.3.3 message is readable, and relax the two assertions. Smaller, but error positions on 3.3.3 still point at the start of the operand.

I'd lean toward 1. Happy to open a PR for whichever you prefer.

Thanks for looking. Fair concern, so I measured it. The setup was one Linux machine with local ext4, pyarrow 25.0.1, comparing this branch against the `open_output_stream` on main. I ran each case 200 times (20 for 10 MB) and repeated the whole run on two disks.

Per file, write + close, median:

| size | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1 KB | 0.16 ms | 3–4 ms |
| 100 KB | 0.5 ms | 3.5–5 ms |
| 10 MB | 17–29 ms | 38–45 ms |

The first file written into a new directory pays one more directory fsync, about +3 ms.

End to end, I timed `table.append()` of 1k rows through `SqlCatalog`: a data file, manifest, manifest list and metadata.json per commit, 30 commits. The median went from 127 → 161 ms and 153 → 187 ms on one disk. On the other it was 178 → 174 ms, which is within noise.

So the cost is a roughly fixed ~3–5 ms per file. It only applies to `file://` warehouses, since object stores don't go through this path. A few ms is small next to a commit, but it is real for workloads that write many small files.

I think we should raise here instead of returning `None`. Encryption is a v3 feature, and java rejects `encryption.key-id` on pre-v3 tables at creation. Once this is wired into writes, returning `None` would mean writes silently go out as plaintext even though the user asked for encryption.

We should make sure the raise doesn't block loading the table or metadata-only commits, otherwise users can't `remove_properties("encryption.key-id")` to fix it. Pre-v3 tables have no `encryption-keys`, so nothing in them can be encrypted and reads don't need the manager. When we wire this up, the error should only surface when producing a snapshot (write side).

Follow-up: we should reject `encryption.key-id` / `encryption.data-key-length` on pre-v3 tables at create / property update, like java's [`checkCompatibility`](https://github.com/apache/iceberg/blob/fb58513787756dedab6550d6695df36a27acb64e/core/src/main/java/org/apache/iceberg/encryption/EncryptionUtil.java#L207-L219).

Hi @azwanzuharimi, thanks for testing this! I agree yours covers all three paths, this one was intentionally scoped to just the initial scan.

That scan is the step that decides which files get read, so this PR keeps its filter simple on purpose: per-column min/max bounds, which always prune by file stats no matter how many keys there are, and the exact matching happens after. A flat In doesn't have that property. Over 200 values it skips stats-based pruning (IN_PREDICATE_LIMIT), so once every key column has over 200 unique keys, which is pretty low for a real upsert, you end up scanning every file in the matched partitions or the whole table.

So I'd rather not close this yet. ANDing these bounds onto the Ins keeps pruning without making the filter deep. If #4027 implements these bounds specifically for the file filtering, I'm happy to close this one.
